slides.title: Pure Functions and Side Effects
slides.prompt: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input arguments and causes no side effects (such as modifying global variables or mutating input arguments).
slides.codeSnippet:
# Pure Function
def add_pure(a, b):
    return a + b

# Impure Function (Side effect)
total = 0
def add_impure(a):
    global total
    total += a
    return total

slides.title: Identifying Side Effects
slides.prompt: Which of the following operations constitutes a side effect in Python?
options: Modifying a list passed into the function in-place
Returning a new tuple calculated from inputs
Performing arithmetic addition on local variables
Declaring a local variable inside the function body
slides.correctAnswer: Modifying a list passed into the function in-place

slides.title: Benefits of Pure Functions
slides.prompt: What is a major advantage of using pure functions in functional programming?
options: They are easier to test, debug, and refactor because they don't depend on external state
They run faster than any object-oriented methods automatically
They bypass Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
slides.correctAnswer: They are easier to test, debug, and refactor because they don't depend on external state

slides.title: Immutability and Hashability
slides.prompt: Why can tuples be used as dictionary keys while lists cannot?
options: Tuples are immutable and hashable, whereas lists are mutable and unhashable
Tuples store elements faster than lists
slides.correctAnswer: Tuples are immutable and hashable, whereas lists are mutable and unhashable
